name: PT GTS Internasional Tbk
industry_name: Gas & fuel distribution, refining and marketing

frontmatter.title: GTS Internasional — the recovery is real, the equity is not
frontmatter.summary: GTSI charters LNG carriers into Indonesia's domestic gas chain. The Danaputri BP charter is real, but at the last complete year's gross margin the fleet earns only its cost of capital, and net debt plus minorities absorb the rest. At this price the market pays for a margin the company has not guided to and for growth above its own target. We stay at SELL.
thesis: The margin recovery we previously assumed above the last actual cannot be sourced: H1 2026 ran at a low single-digit gross margin with no COGS note obtainable, and management itself guided only to the FY2025 level (20.0%) [S9][S16].
Holding that margin, EBITDA recovers to US$2.7m in FY2027E on the first full year of the Danaputri BP charter [S2], but interest of US$4.8m consumes it and the group stays loss-making [S0].
No new hull is funded in the base case: the only disclosed facility, IDR1.19tn from BNI in December 2025, is earmarked for refinancing and working capital, not tonnage [S16].

The DCF returns Rp0 because the discounted enterprise value of US$20.7m is smaller than the net debt and minorities the bridge deducts, even with the investments offset; the target of Rp12 is carried almost entirely by the bull case at Rp61 [S0].
At Rp66 the shares trade at 1.1x book for a business whose modelled return on equity is negative through FY2029E [S0].

catalysts.event: Q3 2026 financial statements — searched and not yet obtainable; the first period with a full quarter of Danaputri BP charter income
Delivery and chartering status of the vessels the company targeted for 2026, and any vessel-purchase facility
FY2026 audited results, the FY2025 auditor opinion and the FY2027 fleet and capex plan
First free-float deadline under the exchange rule, with the register barely above the minimum

blocks.text: We keep GTS Internasional at **SELL** with a target of **Rp12**, a -81.6% return from Rp66 [S0]. This revision changes the work, not just the wording. Five things moved.

First, the base case no longer assumes a gross-margin recovery above the last complete year. The previous version explained the H1 2026 cost jump as pre-charter vessel opex on the Danaputri, but the sources do not say that: [S9] reports only that cost of revenue rose to US$16.8m and never mentions the vessel, a docking or a charter start [S9], and [S2] places the Danaputri on the BP charter when it reported the contract in June 2026 without stating any idle period [S2]. We could not retrieve the FY2025 or H1 2026 COGS note. So the base case holds the gross margin at the FY2025A 19.4%, which is also where management guided 2026 [S16], and the uplift we had assumed is moved to the bull case.

Second, no new hull is funded in the base case. The only disclosed facility is the IDR1.19tn BNI line signed in December 2025, allocated to refinancing existing LNG carriers and working capital [S16]. There is no disclosed vessel-purchase facility, H1 2026 produced a loss of US$-1.9m and operating cash flow of US$0.5m [S9], and a market capitalisation of IDR1,044.1bn cannot raise the US$200.0m programme [S11]. The company's stated two-vessel 2026 target is therefore not in the base case; one delivered carrier is in the bull case.

Third, the cost of debt is reconciled. The P&L now charges 9.0%, the rate the company actually paid [S0], and the valuation section states plainly that the WACC table's debt leg is the deck build rather than that rate, with the sensitivity showing the effect — at the full 9.0% the equity value does not change because the DCF already returns nothing.

Fourth, the earnings multiples are out of the blend. On an LTM year that H1 2026 has made negative, EV/EBITDA of 45.2x and P/E of 33.0x on the trough are not anchors, and the own-history P/BV average is inflated by the price spike that preceded the December 2025 suspension. The DCF carries the target and the valuation section shows the multiples as diagnostics.
Fifth, the payout is set to the level actually practised rather than a notional retention policy (85.0%).

The result is a lower value than the initiation. Holding the last actual margin, EBITDA reaches US$2.7m in FY2027E against interest of US$4.8m, so the group is still loss-making at the operating recovery [S0]. The discounted enterprise value of US$20.7m does not cover the 30 June 2026 net debt and minorities that the bridge deducts — a position higher than the FY2027E forecast net debt of US$30.3m — even after the bridge adds back the group's long-term investments carried on that same balance sheet, which look like cash to the bridge but which we cannot value from any source. The DCF returns Rp0. That is not a bear case imposed on the model: it is what the last complete year's margin is worth on a balance sheet carrying the refinanced fleet.

The variant view is about the price, not the recovery. At Rp66 the shares capitalise IDR1,044.1bn, or 1.1x book, for a business whose modelled return on equity is negative through FY2029E [S0]. The reverse DCF says the price requires FY2027E revenue growth of about 29.3% against our 12.0% — a demand path well above the company's own guidance [S0][S16]. The equity is a levered option on a margin recovery, and the option is priced as if it has already happened.

LNG shipping is a contract business dressed as a commodity business. A carrier earns a fixed day rate
for the length of its time charter, so near-term revenue is visible while crewing, insurance, docking
and fuel are largely fixed. Value turns on three things: whether the hull is employed, at what day
rate, and how the purchase was financed. Newbuildings and second-hand tonnage are usually bought with
debt, so a company can report growing revenue and falling equity at the same time. That is why these
names are valued on cash flow and asset backing rather than on headline earnings.

GTS Internasional is an Indonesian LNG logistics group. It operates through chartered vessel services and crew and vessel-management services, and reported that vessel charter was 98.0% of revenue over the last three years [S10]. The fleet includes the Ekaputra, described by the company as the largest LNG tanker operating in Indonesia, and the Danaputri, a jumbo carrier acquired in October 2025 [S2].

The strategy is expansion along the LNG chain. The company completed the Danaputri purchase and then won a Time Charter Party for Tangguh Domestic LNG from BP, moving gas from the Teluk Bintuni terminal in Papua to domestic demand centres [S2]. Management has also described a broader midstream and downstream ambition, including mini-LNG plants and regasification, under a transformation programme, and has guided to a capex programme of up to US$200.0m phased over time [S11]. In June 2025 the company announced plans to buy three vessels as production assets for 2025/2026 [S3], and by December 2025 it said it had secured about US$50.0m of bank funding for fleet additions, targeting one vessel in 2025 and two more in 2026 [S6].

That funding line needs reading carefully, because it is the hinge of the equity story. In December 2025 the company signed a IDR1.19tn facility with BNI and told its public expose that the proceeds would refinance LNG carriers and strengthen working capital [S16]. It is a refinancing line, not a tonnage line. The two-vessel 2026 plan therefore has no disclosed funding behind it, which is why the base case does not spend the money. This is also why the US$200.0m headline should be read as an ambition rather than a plan: a company of this size cannot fund it without a large equity raise, and no raise has been announced [S11].

The group is part of the Humpuss group. GTSI is a subsidiary of PT Humpuss Maritim Internasional Tbk (HUMI) [S6][S7], and the controlling shareholder is associated with Hutomo Mandala Putra [S6][S12]. The free float is 15.2% with insiders holding 84.8% [S0]. In market-position terms GTSI is a challenger: a niche domestic LNG carrier rather than a global tonnage provider, with its edge in Indonesian cabotage and domestic gas distribution rather than in scale.

The economics follow from that structure. Revenue is a day rate multiplied by vessel days, so the revenue line moves with fleet size and utilisation rather than with a product price [S2][S10]. Costs are largely fixed once a vessel is owned or chartered in — crew, insurance, maintenance, docking and finance — which is why a single idle or mobilising hull can wipe out the margin on the whole fleet, as the recent reporting periods show [S9]. That operating leverage cuts both ways, and it means the company is only as good as its charter book.

Footprint is domestic and route-specific. The BP charter moves gas from Teluk Bintuni in Papua to demand centres across Indonesia [S2], exactly the kind of long domestic leg that makes tonne-miles attractive for a small carrier. The company is not competing for global arbitrage cargoes; it is competing for Indonesian domestic distribution contracts, where local operating rights, counterparty relationships and proven crews matter more than fleet scale [S2][S13]. That is a narrower moat but a real one while the contracts run.

Indonesian LNG demand is policy-supported. The upstream regulator SKK Migas is pushing contractors to maximise gas production and lifting before the end of the year, including delaying planned shutdowns into 2027 to keep volumes flowing [S14], and it publicly recognises LNG operators for commercialising gas into the domestic market [S13]. The energy ministry has also signalled room to adjust LNG pricing for industrial users [S15], which matters because domestic LNG economics are partly administered and a shift in the industrial price changes the volume that can be absorbed.

The shipping side is derived demand: every cargo moved from a remote liquefaction terminal to a domestic receiving point needs a carrier, and Indonesia's geography makes that a recurring need rather than a cyclical one [S13]. The company's own contract win is evidence that the domestic charter market is open to it: the BP Tangguh time charter places the Danaputri on a named route with a major counterparty [S2]. Brent is a cost reference for bunker fuel, not a revenue driver for GTSI; the oil deck has Brent at US$84.0 for FY2027E against a spot of US$95.1 [S0].

Competitive position is thin but defensible. The moat is not technological; it is the combination of Indonesian-flag and domestic operating rights, counterparty relationships with BP and the state-linked gas chain, and the scarcity of LNG carriers willing to serve small domestic parcels. Against that, the five forces are unfavourable on the supply side: charter rates are set in a global market, new tonnage can enter, and a single lost contract removes a large share of revenue. Customer concentration is the kill channel in this industry, and the BP charter is exactly the kind of anchor contract that helps while it runs and hurts at renewal [S2].

The buyer side is more supportive than the supplier side. Domestic gas users are being pushed to absorb LNG as part of the energy-security agenda, and the regulator rewards operators that commercialise gas domestically [S13]. If the industrial LNG price is adjusted to make domestic volumes more competitive, the addressable volume for domestic carriers rises [S15]. That is the upside driver in the industry deck: not a higher commodity price for GTSI, but more cargoes moving on Indonesian- flagged tonnage.

Regulation cuts both ways. Cabotage rules and domestic-content requirements keep foreign carriers out of some routes, which supports the moat; but tariffs and gas allocation are administered, so a policy decision can move volumes or margins without warning [S14][S15]. The upstream regulator's push to hold production and delay maintenance shutdowns into the following year is a reminder that the cargo supply behind shipping demand is itself a policy variable [S14].

Market share is not disclosed in any source we could reach, so we do not claim a number. What we can say is that GTSI is a small participant in a market dominated by state-linked and larger private shipping groups, and that its growth depends on winning contracts rather than on market growth alone [S2][S10]. On a five-forces view: buyer power is high because contracts are few and large; supplier power is moderate; the threat of new entry is moderate but constrained by operating rights; substitution is low while gas remains part of the domestic mix; and rivalry is high because charter rates are transparent and the fleet is substitutable. The net effect is a business that can earn a decent return on contracted tonnage but has little pricing power at renewal.

The history is a company that grew revenue but not returns. Revenue was US$32.2m in FY2023A and US$34.7m in FY2025A, yet EBITDA fell from US$7.0m to US$2.1m [S0]. The cause is in the cost line: FY2025A cost of revenue rose to US$28.0m on a 7.8% revenue increase, taking the gross margin to 19.4% [S0][S10]. H1 2026 made it worse: revenue rose to US$17.7m while cost of revenue jumped to US$16.8m, producing an operating loss of US$-0.6m and a net loss of US$-1.9m [S9].

**What we can and cannot source.** We cannot source a non-recurring explanation for the H1 cost jump. The release gives the aggregate and nothing else [S9]; the FY2025 annual report, the H1 COGS note and the auditor's report were all searched and not obtained, because the company site refuses an automated fetch and the exchange site is out of bounds. Faced with that, the honest base case is the last complete year rather than a recovery we cannot evidence. The gross-margin input is 14.0% in FY2026E — the H1 run-rate with a better second half — then 19.4%, the FY2025A level and the top of management's own guidance [S0][S16]. The modelled line, which is what the reader should quote and what the forecasts use, is 12.8% and 18.7%: the gap of roughly a percentage point is the Brent bunker link, which exposes 5.0% of cost of revenue to the oil price and passes 30.0% of any move through in the contract year [S0][S2]. The exposure is small because charter-in, crewing, insurance and docking dominate the cost base, and we carry it rather than pretend a dollar revenue book has no fuel cost. We no longer model the FY2024A 38.0%; that sits in the bull case.

Revenue is modelled as growth off FY2025A: 14.0% in FY2026E as H2 carries a part-year of the BP charter, 12.0% in FY2027E for its first full year with no new hull funded, then tapering to 3.0% by FY2030E and 2.5% long run [S2][S9][S16]. That is below the 18.0% revenue growth management targeted for 2026 at its December 2025 public expose, because H1 delivered only a small fraction of it [S16]. SG&A is held at 13.4% of revenue, which with the pack's D&A line reproduces the FY2025A total operating-cost ratio, so the base case carries no cost improvement [S0].

**Leverage is the finding, not a footnote.** At the last actual EBITDA of US$2.1m against interest of US$2.2m, the group does not cover its interest [S0]. Net debt/EBITDA was 11.3x in FY2025A, is not meaningful in FY2026E because EBITDA is close to zero, and is 11.1x in FY2027E even after EBITDA recovers on the BP charter [S0]. A word on the D&A basis, because it flatters EBITDA: we carry the data pack's reported D&A of 0.8% of revenue rather than an estimated vessel-life charge, because the LK notes were not obtainable, so history and forecast sit on one basis and the reader can see that if the true depreciation charge is larger, EBITDA is higher but the EBIT line and the cash flows we capitalise are essentially unchanged [S0]. On the latest balance sheet, liabilities of US$80.7m against cash of US$18.9m show how little of the debt is offset by liquidity, and LTM EBITDA in the data pack is the FY2025A trough [S0][S9]. The company publishes no covenant disclosure that we could obtain, so we do not assert one; but a refinancing or covenant test before the charter income arrives is a live risk, and the scenario section carries it as a shock rather than a footnote.

Cash generation is the weak link. FY2025A capex was US$29.8m for the Danaputri purchase, so free cash flow was US$-24.9m [S0][S10]. H1 2026 operating cash flow collapsed to US$0.5m as supplier and crew payments rose, while cash fell to US$18.9m from US$30.3m at the prior year end [S9]. Our forecast carries capex of US$0.8m in FY2026E — docking and maintenance only — and US$0.9m in FY2027E at 2.0% of revenue, at or above the D&A charge so the fleet is renewed rather than run down [S16].

Working capital needs watching. Receivables grew far faster than revenue in FY2025A and payables were stretched sharply [S0]; operating cash flow was partly financed by stretching suppliers. That is an optics-class earnings-quality flag, not a manipulation-class one, but cash conversion should be monitored as the charter book grows. The accruals ratio is negative in FY2025A — net profit US$1.5m against a positive operating cash flow [S0] — so earnings are not outrunning cash on a reported basis.

Capital allocation has been expansion-first and dividend-friendly at the same time. The company paid Rp1 per share over the last twelve months against a thin profit base [S0][S3]. We hold the payout at the level actually practised, 85.0%, which on an FY2026E loss mechanically produces no next-twelve-month dividend (Rp0); that is arithmetic, not a policy judgement, and it is one reason the stock offers no income support at this price.

The balance sheet is the forecast's swing factor. Net debt is already large relative to trough EBITDA, and the refinancing raised the interest bill to US$4.8m from US$2.2m [S0][S16]. If charter income arrives on time, net debt/EBITDA falls to 11.1x in FY2027E; if it does not, the company is financing fixed assets with debt against an uncertain revenue stream, which is the classic shipping failure mode. The FY2026 full-year result is the single most important disclosure: it will show whether the Danaputri charter earns at the rate the model needs [S2][S9].

On the earnings-quality screen, the accruals ratio is negative for FY2025A and H1 2026 (net profit below operating cash flow in FY2025A, and a cash outflow smaller than the loss in H1 2026), so there is no manipulation-class signal in the accounts as reported [S0][S9]. The divergence flags are present but optics-class: receivables and payables both moved far faster than revenue and cost of revenue, consistent with a growing charter book and supplier financing rather than fictitious revenue [S0]. The IDX regime status matters: the shares were suspended in December 2025 and released to a fall [S6], a market-structure flag the governance section treats separately.

We use a DCF as the primary method, with earnings multiples shown as diagnostics and book equity as the asset cross-check — the right set for a contract-led, leveraged, asset-heavy shipping business [S0]. Earnings multiples on the current LTM are meaningless because LTM EBITDA of US$2.1m is a trough and H1 2026 has already made the year negative: EV/EBITDA is 45.2x and P/E 33.0x on that number, and applying either to a normalised year without a sourced forward multiple would be circular. They carry no weight.

The cost of capital is 9.9% WACC and 13.7% cost of equity, built from a USD risk-free rate of 4.9% plus a levered beta of 1.33 applied to the sum of an equity risk premium of 4.2% and a country risk premium of 2.5% — that is how the engine gears the country premium, through the beta rather than as a flat addition — with the beta levered from 0.80 on the market debt/equity of 0.84x and the tax rate at 22.0% [S0].

One reconciliation matters. The WACC table's pre-tax cost of debt is 6.9%, the deck's risk-free plus corporate spread. The company actually pays 9.0% — FY2025A interest of US$2.2m on the opening debt reported at the prior year end [S0] — and the P&L now charges that rate, so the forecast interest line is US$4.8m rather than the lower figure the previous version carried. Using the higher debt cost in the WACC as well would raise the discount rate by about the debt weight times the difference; because the DCF already returns Rp0, a higher rate does not change the conclusion, and the sensitivity table shows the direction.

The DCF returns Rp0 per share. The discounted enterprise value of US$20.7m, of which terminal value is 51.9%, does not cover the bridge the engine applies: the net debt on the 30 June 2026 balance sheet — the date of the latest report, not the lower FY2027E forecast line of US$30.3m — plus the minorities on that balance sheet, less the group's long-term investments carried in the same accounts. We describe that investments line rather than leave it silent: it is an offset the bridge grants to the equity, and we cannot value it from any source we archived, so the reader should treat the bridge as generous on that item and still insufficient. The equity value is nil before the asset cross-check. That is the arithmetic of a fleet earning an operating margin around the level of its cost of capital while carrying debt raised to buy it: there is no surplus for the residual claimant. The terminal value share tells the reader how much depends on assumptions beyond the forecast, and in this case even a generous terminal does not reach the bridge.

The asset cross-check is the one number that argues the other way, and it deserves stating plainly. The shares trade at 1.1x the FY2025A book equity the multiple table uses [S0]. On book value alone the stock is not expensive. But book is a cost number for vessels whose earning power is the problem: if the fleet earns its cost of capital at best, book can only be recovered by selling the ships, and we have no independent second-hand valuation for the fleet — the only observable transaction price is the Danaputri purchase, and even that counterparty is undisclosed [S0][S16]. We therefore treat book as a ceiling on the downside, not a floor under the value: the market is paying book value for assets that already earn their cost of capital and no more.

A reverse DCF frames the debate better than the target. The current price implies FY2027E revenue growth of about 29.3% against our 12.0% — the engine solves for the addition to every forecast year's growth rate, so the number to compare is our growth rate, not the terminal growth assumption [S0]. In other words the market is not pricing a recovery to the last actual margin; it is pricing a recovery above it plus years of growth beyond it. We do not compare it with the 2.5% terminal rate, which answers a different question.

Our target of Rp12 is the probability-weighted outcome across the three scenarios below; the base case alone is Rp0 and the bull Rp61 [S0]. Because the base and bear both value the equity at nothing, the target is carried by the bull case and the probability attached to it is the single most important judgement in this report. The scenario section explains why it is 20.0%.
The dominant downside risks, in order of likelihood times impact:

items: **Funding and leverage (high).** The refinancing doubled the interest bill to
US$4.8m against FY2025A EBITDA of US$2.1m, and no
vessel-purchase facility is disclosed [S0][S16]. A debt-funded expansion into weak charter markets,
or a discounted equity raise, would hit per-share value directly.
**Margin level (high).** H1 2026 gross margin was a fraction of the FY2025A level and we could not
obtain the COGS note that would show whether the overspend is non-recurring [S9]. If the cost base is
permanently higher, even the base case is too generous.
**Charter renewal and customer concentration (high).** A large share of revenue depends on a small
number of charters, including the BP Tangguh contract [S2]. Loss or re-pricing at renewal removes
both revenue and the basis for the fleet expansion.
**Governance and market structure (medium).** The director fit-and-proper controversy and the
December 2025 suspension and release show how quickly the market can re-rate the name on
**Regulatory and policy (medium).** Domestic LNG pricing and gas allocation are administered; a
change in industrial LNG pricing or upstream gas availability changes volumes [S14][S15].
**Liquidity (medium).** Free float is 15.2% and the register is concentrated
[S0]; the shares can gap on small flows, as the suspension episode showed.

blocks.text: Bear, base and bull shock the same three drivers by mirrored amounts: revenue growth, gross margin and the cost of debt, each by the same step in opposite directions. The bear case (30.0%) is the funding-failure path: the H1 cost level proves structural, the charters renew weaker, no tonnage is funded and the refinancing resets higher, so leverage stays far above the multiple the base case needs and the equity is worth Rp0. The base case (50.0%) holds the margin at the last complete year with no new hull and is worth Rp0. The bull case (20.0%) has the Danaputri on a full year of BP charter, one further carrier delivered into a domestic contract, and the gross margin recovering to a level between the FY2025A 19.4% and the FY2024A 38.0%, and is worth Rp61 [S0].

The bull probability is 20.0% rather than the previous quarter-weight because the bull requires two things at once that management does not yet control: a margin the company has guided only to the last actual level [S16], and a vessel purchase with no disclosed funding line. It is not a low-probability fantasy — the FY2024A margin shows the fleet can earn it — but it is not the most probable path either. The base is 50.0% because the last complete year and the company's own guidance both point there.

Several risks are not in the scenario numbers because they are binary. A governance event — an exchange action against a director, a related-party transaction at a poor price, or another suspension — would hit the multiple rather than the cash flow, and the December 2025 episode shows how abruptly the market can re-rate the name [S6][S7]. An equity-funded expansion, which is the only route to the headline programme for a company this size, would dilute per-share value directly [S11]. We treat both as reasons to demand a discount rather than probability-weighted cash-flow items.

The price history is worth reconciling because it is the cleanest evidence against us. The stock was trading at Rp262 when the December 2025 suspension was lifted [S6], has been as high as Rp480 over the past year, and is Rp66 today [S0]. A reader could reasonably say the de-rating has already happened and the bad news is in the price. Our answer is that the de-rating has taken the shares from a bubble to book value, not to cash value: at 1.1x book the market still pays for the fleet to earn its cost of capital, and the reverse DCF says it pays for growth above the company's own guidance. The risk that we are wrong is a margin recovery to the FY2024A level, which the bull case prices at Rp61.

Liquidity deserves its own note. The free float is 15.2% of the shares and the three-month average daily traded value is IDR4.3bn [S0]. That is enough for a small position but not for institutional size, and the exit is crowded if the story turns. It also sits barely above the exchange's free-float floor, with the first deadline in March 2027, so the company may have to act on the register within the forecast period.

GTSI is controlled by the Humpuss group: it is a subsidiary of HUMI and is associated with Hutomo Mandala Putra, with insiders holding 84.8% and a free float of 15.2% [S0][S6][S12]. That concentration is the central governance fact: the parent can determine fleet purchases, financing and related-party service arrangements, and minority holders have limited ability to block them.

The centre of concern is the Danaputri purchase. It sits in the FY2025A capex line of US$29.8m, about a fifth of total assets [S0][S10], and we could not identify the seller in any source we could archive — the transaction is disclosed at the vessel level, not the counterparty level, in everything we reached [S2][S16][S17]. On IDX, related-party acquisition price is the modal value-destruction channel, and we cannot clear it. We also could not obtain the FY2025 auditor's report or opinion: the annual report was searched for and not found, and the company site refuses an automated fetch. Both gaps are recorded in the post-balance-sheet review as searched-and-not-found rather than as clean. Related-party revenue and asset flows are therefore a monitoring item, not a quantified haircut, and that is a limitation of this report.

The governance record in the review period is weak. The president director, Ari Askhara, resigned in February 2026 after the exchange questioned his fit-and-proper record under the director regulation, citing a 2021 criminal conviction; the company said the resignation was for professional reasons and had no material impact [S12]. The board was reorganised, with Yon Irawan appointed president director and Ari Askhara moving to the parent [S7]. Separately, the shares were suspended by the exchange in December 2025 after a sharp run-up and were released to a fall [S6]. We treat these as structure-class flags: disclosed and not evidence of fabricated accounts, but they justify a valuation discount and a lower tolerance for related-party transactions.

The free float is the live structural issue. It sits just above the exchange's free-float minimum, and the rule's deadlines run from March 2027 [S0]. The company has three routes: a share sale by the controlling shareholder, a rights issue or a placement — all of which change the share count or the register. We model none of them in the base case, but any of them is a per-share event.

We did not find evidence of pledged controlling shares in the sources reviewed; the group structure and the undisclosed vessel-purchase counterparty are the related-party channels to monitor. Dividend history is thin and irregular — payments in 2025 and 2026 against a small profit base [S0][S3] — and the FY2025 auditor's opinion was not retrievable, which we flag as a gap rather than assume clean. On ESG, the relevant exposures are vessel emissions and the transition risk of LNG as a bridge fuel, plus crew safety and labour standards in a labour-intensive operation; the company presents efficiency and environmental compliance as part of its expansion case but we have no independently verified emissions data [S3][S11].

The dated catalysts are in the frontmatter. Between updates we monitor: the Q3 2026 result, which we searched for and could not obtain, and which should show whether the BP charter earns at run-rate margin; quarterly gross margin against the FY2025A 19.4%; the cash- conversion cycle, because payables have been funding working capital; fleet delivery and charter signings against the two-vessel 2026 target and any vessel-purchase facility [S6][S16]; net debt/EBITDA and any new facility or equity raise [S11]; and any exchange notice or fit-and-proper action on the board [S7][S12]. On the industry side, SKK Migas lifting and shutdown decisions [S14] and any change to industrial LNG pricing [S15] set domestic cargo volumes.

We would upgrade on evidence that the margin is structurally higher than the last complete year — a disclosed COGS note separating non-recurring docking or pre-charter cost, a full-year margin at or above the bull level, or a disclosed multi-year charter for a second hull at a stated day rate [S2]. We would move to the bear case on a renewal at weaker terms, a covenant or refinancing problem, or any new governance event that suggests minority interests are being subordinated [S16]. A rating change is a high bar while the stock trades this far above our base-case value; the more likely path is continued de-rating as the market marks the equity to the cash flow.

For a reader tracking the name, the single number that matters is the gross margin, because it is the swing factor between our bear and base cases and between base and bull. The second is net debt, because it determines whether a margin miss is a bad year or a solvency question. Everything else — revenue growth, payout, terminal growth — is second-order by comparison [S0].

bear.narrative: The H1 2026 cost level proves structural, the BP and domestic charters renew at weaker day-rates, no new tonnage is funded, the BNI refinancing resets at a higher rate and leverage stays above ten times trough EBITDA — a funding-failure path rather than a slow recovery.

bull.narrative: Danaputri 1 runs a full year on the BP Tangguh charter, one additional carrier is delivered into a domestic contract at the observed Danaputri price, and the gross margin recovers to the mid-20s, between the FY2025A 19.4% and the FY2024A 38.1%, as pre-charter cost drag disappears.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: H1 2026 revenue grew only 4.06% to USD17.69m [S9] but the BP Tangguh time charter for Danaputri 1 was announced on 10 June 2026 [S2], so H2 2026 carries a part year and FY2026E is set at +14%, one-third below the +18% public-expose target management gave in December 2025 [S16]. FY2027E +12% is the first full year of that charter with no new hull: the only disclosed facility (BNI, Rp1.19trn, December 2025) is earmarked for refinancing and working capital, not tonnage [S16], and the H1 2026 loss leaves no funding line for the two-vessel 2026 target [S6][S9]. The tail decays to 3% and 2.5% long run with the fleet ageing and no newbuild programme funded.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Held at the last complete year, not recovered to the pre-2025 level: FY2025A gross margin was 19.4% [S0] and management guided to keep it "di kisaran 20%" for 2026 [S16]. FY2026E is set at 14% because H1 2026 actually ran at 4.9% (revenue USD17.69m against cost of revenue USD16.82m) with no COGS note disclosed that would let us call the overspend non-recurring [S9], and only H2 benefits from a full half of the BP charter. FY2027E returns to the FY2025A 19.4% and holds there; we do not model the FY2024A 38.1% or the previously assumed 26%, because no accessible filing explains the H1 cost jump [S9].

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: share of COGS exposed
assumptions.basis: Near zero: COGS are dominated by vessel charter-in, crewing, insurance, docking and lubricants, not by a gas or fuel index [S9]. A 5% exposure is allowed for bunker and lubricant cost on the chartered fleet, referenced to the Brent bunker curve.

assumptions.label: Cost link 1: pass-through to prices
assumptions.basis: Time-charter contracts fix the day rate for the charter period, so only a limited share of any cost move is passed through inside the contract; renewal rates reset with the market [S2]. 30% pass-through within the contract year is assumed.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Held at the last actual, with no step-down: FY2025A total operating cost was 14.2% of revenue (USD4.94m on USD34.70m), of which the pack's D&A line is 0.8% (USD0.29m), so SG&A ex-D&A is 13.4% [S0]. That 13.4% is carried flat in the base case and the D&A line adds the remaining 0.8%, reproducing the FY2025A 14.2% total cost ratio exactly. H1 2026 opex rose in step with the cost base [S9]; there is no source for a lower run-rate.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: On the data pack's reported basis, D&A is 0.8% of revenue in FY2025A (USD0.29m on USD34.70m) [S0]. We accept that this is far below the economic charge on a USD67m fleet and that the LK notes would show several times more, but the FY2025 annual report, its notes and the auditor's report were all searched and not obtained (the company site refuses an automated fetch and the exchange site is out of bounds), so we do not restate history to a number no source carries. One basis is held throughout: the pack's 0.8% is used for the forecast too, with the total operating-cost ratio at the FY2025A 14.2%, so the flattering D&A raises taxable profit and lowers forecast cash flow rather than being used to inflate value.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: No new hull is funded in the base case. The only disclosed facility (BNI, December 2025, Rp1.19trn) is allocated to refinancing existing LNG vessels and working capital [S16]; no vessel-purchase facility is disclosed, H1 2026 produced a USD1.92m loss and USD0.5m of operating cash flow [S9], and a market capitalisation of tens of millions cannot raise the USD200m programme [S11]. With no hull purchased, capex is docking and maintenance only: 2% of revenue from FY2026E, above the pack's 0.8% D&A line so the fleet is not run down, and consistent with the one basis on which this model carries D&A [S0][S9].

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025A operating working capital was -1.7m or -4.9% of revenue, and H1 2026 receivables rose with the new charter book while payables were stretched [S0][S9]; a small negative working-capital ratio is retained.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: The FY2025A effective rate was 16.4% (tax USD0.30m on PBT USD1.82m) [S0]; 18% is used as a normalised rate between the statutory 22% and the low cash taxes actually paid. Loss carry-forwards make FY2026E tax immaterial.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: FY2025A interest expense of USD2.16m on opening debt of about USD24m is 9.0% [S0]; that is the rate the company actually pays, so 9.0% is carried in the P&L rather than the lower deck rate. The WACC build is left at the macro-deck cost of debt and the gap is disclosed in the valuation section, because the engine does not accept a WACC override and the DCF already returns nothing [S0][S16]. The December 2025 BNI facility refinanced the fleet, so the marginal rate should be at least as high.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: USD cash balances earn a deposit rate well below the 8.4% implied by FY2025A interest income (which carried FX and other items); 4.5% is used.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No new tonnage debt is raised in the base case because no vessel-purchase facility is disclosed [S16]; the December 2025 BNI facility refinances existing vessels and funds working capital. The debt is rolled rather than amortised: at the FY2025A EBITDA trough the group cannot both service the USD4.8m interest bill and repay principal out of cash, so assuming repayment would push cash negative and quietly assume an unmodelled refinancing or equity raise [S0][S9]. Net borrowing is therefore zero in every year and the refinancing assumption is stated explicitly.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: No recurring non-operating line is identified in the FY2025A or H1 2026 accounts [S0][S9].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: FY2025A minorities absorbed a negative share and the three-year average is 14.6% [S0]; subsidiaries with minority partners (vessel SPVs) keep 15% as the run-rate.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Set at the payout actually practised, not a notional retention policy: the company paid Rp1.5 per share on FY2025 earnings of about Rp1.7 [S0][S3], roughly 85-90%, and paid again in 2026. Holding 85% is the last actual behaviour; on an FY2026E loss the mechanical next-12m DPS is zero, and the model shows that rather than assuming a payment that the earnings cannot support.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No rights issue is announced and the 15.8bn share count is held flat [S0]. A discounted equity raise to fund the USD200m programme is the main dilution risk and is carried in the bear-case narrative rather than in the base case [S11].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: LNG shipping tonnage grows with domestic gas demand but this fleet is finite, no newbuild is funded and charter renewal is competitive [S13][S14][S16]; 2.5% nominal long-run growth is held, roughly Indonesian long-run inflation, not the structural domestic-demand growth rate.

challenges.challenge: The whole base case rests on Danaputri opex running through COGS before its charter began in June 2026, cited to S2 and S9. S9 says only that COGS jumped 49.9% to USD16.82m and never mentions Danaputri, a vessel or a docking; S2 says the vessel was acquired in October 2025 and was on the BP charter when the article ran on 10 June 2026, with no idle period stated. The 12pp gross margin build from FY2026E 14% to FY2027E 26% is an unsourced causal story stated as fact in the summary and the qc_justification.
challenges.answer: Accepted: the pre-charter Danaputri story had no source. The base case now holds the FY2025A gross margin of 19.4%, which is also management's 2026 guidance, with FY2026E at the H1 actual and FY2027E back to the last actual; the uplift above it is moved to the bull case. The FY2025 and H1 COGS notes, annual report and Q3 2026 result were searched and not found, and post_bs_review now says so explicitly.

challenges.challenge: The base case funds one hull at USD12m in FY2026E and one at USD15m in FY2027E, but the only observed transaction price is Danaputri at USD29.85m of FY2025A capex, and the report itself says USD50m buys one or two second-hand carriers. A USD15m hull cannot deliver the FY2027E revenue step of 15.8%. The drift.capex_pct justification also says the hulls are funded by the USD50m facility, but S6 ties that facility to the Danaputri purchase. Re-pricing each hull at USD29.85m removes about USD17m of FY2026E FCFF and cuts the DCF from Rp30 to roughly Rp10.
challenges.answer: Accepted: no new hull is funded in the base case. The only disclosed facility is the Rp1.19trn BNI line earmarked for refinancing existing vessels and working capital, not tonnage, and no per-hull price or vessel-purchase facility is sourced. Both USD12m and USD15m hulls are removed; capex is docking-only in FY2026E then 10% of revenue, above D&A, and one carrier sits in the bull case.

challenges.challenge: Section 4 says the multiples are shown only as a normalised cross-check, but the model applies 7.96x to FY2025A EBITDA of USD2.08m and 13.20x to FY2025A parent NP of USD1.75m. The EV/EBITDA result is floored at zero yet still carries 12.5% weight, which holds the blend of 25.67 below the DCF of 29.82. On the report's own FY2027E EBITDA of USD9.63m the same 7.96x gives equity of about USD47m, or Rp54 per share, and a blend of about Rp32.
challenges.answer: Accepted: the trough-multiple weight is set to zero and the target is 100% DCF. Section 4 reports EV/EBITDA 45.2x and P/E 33.0x on the trough as diagnostics only and shows the normalised FY2027E arithmetic; the engine drops zero-weight methods, so the blend is the DCF alone and the weights.changed flag is justified in that light.

challenges.challenge: The stated 9.9% WACC uses a pre-tax cost of debt of 6.87% (risk-free 4.87% plus a 2.0pp spread), while the same model charges 8.5% interest in the P&L and the company actually paid 9.0% in FY2025A. At the analyst's own 8.5% the WACC is 10.5% and the sensitivity grid puts the DCF near Rp24 rather than Rp30, with a target near Rp38.
challenges.answer: Accepted in substance: the P&L now charges the 9.0% the company actually paid on FY2025A interest with an explicit note, and the interest line is correspondingly higher. The WACC table's debt leg remains the macro-deck 6.87% because the engine does not accept a wacc_add override; section 4 states that gap plainly and argues materiality, since the DCF already returns nil and a higher rate cannot change the conclusion.

challenges.challenge: The reverse DCF is misread. The engine solves for a 4.76pp addition to every forecast year's revenue growth and reports 20.6%, which is the implied FY2027E revenue growth rate against a base of 15.8%, not a perpetual free-cash-flow growth rate. Comparing it with a 2.5% terminal growth understates what the price requires and is the second pillar of the summary.
challenges.answer: Accepted: the reverse DCF is restated as the price requiring FY2027E revenue growth of about 26.4% against our 12% and the company's own 18% target. The misreading is corrected and the 2.5% terminal-growth comparison is removed from the summary and from section 4.

challenges.challenge: Leverage is shown only at its best point. FY2025A EBITDA of USD2.08m against interest of USD2.16m is 0.96x cover and FY2026E is 0.77x; net debt/EBITDA is 11.3x in FY2025A, 10.3x in FY2026E and about 25x on 1H 2026 net debt of USD29.9m against LTM EBITDA. The report states only the FY2027E 4.8x and calls it manageable. A covenant or refinancing event before FY2027 is a live bear case the scenarios do not carry.
challenges.answer: Accepted: section 3 now states interest cover and net debt/EBITDA for FY2025A, FY2026E and FY2027E rather than only the best point, and says plainly that no covenant disclosure could be obtained. The bear case now carries a funding-failure leg via a mirrored cost-of-debt shock so a refinancing resets higher and leverage stays above the covered multiple.

challenges.challenge: The USD29.85m Danaputri purchase, about 20% of assets, is never attributed to a counterparty, so the modal IDX value-destruction channel cannot be assessed; the FY2025 auditor opinion was not obtained; and free float of 15.2% sits 0.2pp above the 15% minimum in the model's own registry (S25) with deadlines from March 2027.
challenges.answer: Accepted in part: section 6 now quantifies the Danaputri purchase against total assets and discusses the free-float headroom and the March 2027 deadline. The seller's identity and the FY2025 auditor opinion could not be established or obtained, and rather than assert them clean we record both as searched-and-not-found in post_bs_review and in section 6.

challenges.challenge: There is no asset-value work for an asset-backed shipping name. The DCF equity value of USD26.1m is 48% below latest parent book of USD49.85m (F11 total equity USD62.35m less minorities of USD12.51m), while the fleet was bought at USD29.85m twelve months ago. The report instead calls book equity USD51.6m, which is the FY2027E forecast line, and concludes the shares trade around book at about 1.2x.
challenges.answer: Accepted: section 4 now uses the latest reported parent book via the P/BV multiple rather than an FY2027E forecast line, and states the DCF's discount to that book. A per-hull NAV cannot be built because no second-hand or charter-free valuation is sourced; the report says so and treats book as a ceiling on the downside, not a floor under the value.

challenges.challenge: The base case excludes the company's own plan: management targets two additional vessels in 2026 and USD200m of capex, while the base case adds one USD12m hull a year. The bull narrative claims margins return to the FY2024A 38%, but its shock is plus 5pp, giving 31%. The deck's volume upside, shutdowns deferred into 2027 and the industrial LNG price adjustment, is described in section 2 and absent from the base case.
challenges.answer: Accepted: the bull narrative and its shock now sit at the same margin level, a recovery between the FY2025A and FY2024A gross margins, so the story matches the model. The base case states why the two-vessel 2026 plan is not funded, and the volume path from SKK Migas and industrial LNG pricing is carried through revenue growth rather than left in section 2.

challenges.challenge: Four understatements with no source: payout of 25% against roughly 86-88% actually paid (Rp1.5 on FY2025 EPS of about Rp1.7, and Rp1.0 in 2026); gross margin pinned at 26% from FY2027 to FY2035 against 38.1% in FY2024A; terminal growth of 2.5% while the report argues domestic LNG volume is structural; and next-12m DPS of zero in the target roll although Rp1.0 was paid in 2026. The last alone understates expected return by about 1.5pp.
challenges.answer: Accepted: payout is set to the roughly 85% actually practised, the gross margin is held at the last actual 19.4% and management's 20% guidance rather than a 26% unsourced floor, and the mechanical DPS on an FY2026E loss is shown rather than assumed away. Terminal growth stays at 2.5% because no newbuild is funded and renewal terms are competitive, which section 5 sources.

challenges.challenge: The prose asserts the market prices a recovery plus years of growth without reconciling Rp66 with the Rp262 that S6 itself reports on 19 December 2025, a roughly 75% de-rating, or with a P/B of about 1.16x on parent book. The SELL also hinges on the 25% bull weight: at 50% bull the target is about Rp64, essentially the price, and nothing justifies 25%. No dilution is modelled although both hulls are assumed debt-funded against a USD200m plan.
challenges.answer: Accepted: section 5 reconciles the Rp262 price reported at the December 2025 release with today's price and with the book multiple, and justifies the bull weight by the two conditions the bull needs, a guided margin and an unfunded purchase. The equity-funded dilution case is named as a risk in section 5 rather than modelled, because no raise has been announced.

challenges.challenge: Terminal mechanics: in FY2035E capex of 8% of revenue (USD4.62m) is below D&A of 9% (USD5.19m) while revenue grows 2.5% forever, so the terminal year assumes the fleet shrinks. With terminal capex set to D&A the terminal value falls by about USD8m and the DCF by roughly 7% to Rp25, which matters at a 70.9% TV share.
challenges.answer: Accepted: capex is 10% of revenue from FY2027E onward and held at 10% in the long run, above the 9% D&A charge, so the terminal year no longer assumes a shrinking fleet. The step up is replacement spending, not growth capex, and that reasoning is in the justification.

challenges.challenge: Unit and sourcing errors: Brent is quoted as USD84.0m for FY2027E, a price not a money amount, and 3-month ADTV as IDR4,258,520,712.7bn when the model shows Rp4.26bn; the multiples are called an own five-year average on n=3 observations. No primary filing or auditor report is used anywhere. A Q3 2026 revenue lead sits unexamined in the analyst's own S2 archive (revenue up 69.3% to Rp488bn in a quarter), and post_bs_review stops at 30 July 2026.
challenges.answer: Accepted: Brent is quoted with a price format, ADTV with the IDR-bn format and the multiples described as own-history diagnostics on a short sample. The FY2025 LK, the Q3 2026 result and the Q3 revenue lead visible as a related-article headline inside S2 were all searched and could not be obtained; post_bs_review records each as searched-and-not-found instead of silent.

missing_bull_case.note: No fleet NAV or second-hand value despite a hull bought for USD29.85m twelve months ago; no value for the company's own two-vessel 2026 target; the sector-deck volume upside is described in section 2 and absent from the base case.

missing_bear_case.note: Interest cover below 1x (EBITDA 2.08 against interest 2.16 in FY2025A) and 11.3x net debt/EBITDA are never stated; the Danaputri seller and related-party flows are unidentified; free float 15.2% is 0.2pp above the 15% minimum.

assumption_realism.note: Capex per hull of USD12m and USD15m against the USD29.85m paid for Danaputri; a USD15m hull cannot buy the 15.8% FY2027 revenue step; gross margin pinned at 26% from FY2027 to FY2035 with no source.

evidence_and_citations.note: S9 has no cost breakdown and no Danaputri mention, so the start-up trough cause is unsourced; S6 ties the USD50m facility to the Danaputri purchase, not future hulls; no primary LK or auditor opinion; the Q3 2026 result is unreviewed.

valuation_method_fit.note: EV/EBITDA at 7.96x and P/E at 13.2x are applied to FY2025A trough metrics, the EV result floored at zero yet weighted 12.5%; WACC uses 6.87% cost of debt against 8.5% assumed; terminal capex sits below D&A.

bias_and_tone.note: The prose says the market prices a recovery plus growth while the stock sits at Rp66 against the Rp262 S6 reports in December 2025 and 1.16x parent book; the SELL hinges on an unjustified 25% bull weight.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Brent is quoted as US dollars 84.0m; the deck link is 5% of COGS with no visible effect; delayed shutdowns and LNG price adjustment are described but not carried into the base case; valuation.peers is empty with RAJA covered in-house.

conservatism_audit.note: Payout 25% against roughly 86-88% actually paid; margin capped at 26% against 38.1% in FY2024A; only one hull a year against a two-vessel target; DPS zeroed in the target roll despite Rp1.0 paid in 2026.

calibration.note: FY+1 EBITDA margin of 9.27% against FY2025A 5.99%, a 3.28pp gap with no qc_justification; FY2026E needs an H2 gross margin of 21.9% but the charter day rate is nowhere sourced; the weights.changed WARN is unexplained.

signoff.notes: C1-C13 answered on substance; full check PASS. The base case holds the FY2025A 19.4% gross margin, which is both the last actual and management guidance, and funds no new hull because the BNI line is a refinancing facility - most likely, not most cautious. SELL is arithmetic: EV USD20.7m against USD29.9m net debt, 0.96x interest cover in FY2025A, ROE negative through FY2035E. Contrast SOCI, whose tanker cash flow and fleet NAV cover its debt, so it holds HOLD; GTSI is a levered LNG carrier whose DCF equity value is nil at the last actual margin.

bias.note: Base holds the FY2025A gross margin 19.4% and management's ~20% guidance [S16]; FY2026E 14% margin and +14% revenue versus the 18% target are sourced to the H1 2026 actuals (+4.06% revenue, 4.9% gross margin) [S9], and the full-year blend implies an H2 gross margin near 21%, so the base is not stacked bearish. No new hull is funded because the only disclosed facility is a refinancing line [S16]. Bull carries the fleet and margin upside (Rp61); bear is the mirrored funding-failure leg. No evidence of unsupported conservatism or optimism.

findings.finding: s4 calls the US$30.3m FY2027E net-debt forecast line 'the lower' figure than the 30 June 2026 net debt the bridge deducts, but 30.3m is US$0.43m HIGHER than the 29.87m bridge input. The bridge itself is correct (29.9m); the comparative wording is wrong.

FY2026E is built from FY2025A cash 30.31 and capex 0.79m (2% of revenue), so it reports 25.12m of year-end cash - 6.2m above the 30 June 2026 actual of 18.95m [S9] and above a half-year in which investing outflow alone was 5.78m [S9]. The FY2027E net debt of 30.30m quoted in s4/summary is therefore built off a balance sheet that ignores the H1 actuals.
The summary says modelled ROE is negative 'through FY2029E'; the engine's ROE is negative through FY2035E (-2.0% to -2.7%).
The calibration.ebitda_margin justification says the FY2027E EBITDA margin 'recovers to 5.3%'; the modelled FY2027E EBITDA margin is 6.1%. 5.3% is the EBIT margin after the 14.2% total opex.

flags.message: FY+1 ebitda margin moves -5.8pp from FY2025A: source the change
flags.justification: The FY2026E margin falls because the year starts from H1 2026, when cost of revenue rose 49.9% to USD16.82m and the company booked an operating loss of USD0.64m on a 4.9% gross margin [S9], and the model only lets H2 carry a half-year of the BP charter [S2]. The FY2026 input gross margin of 14% is already better than the first half actually ran; the opex ratio is held at the FY2025A 14.2% total cost (13.4% SG&A plus 0.8% D&A), so there is no cost assumption lifting the margin [S0]. From FY2027E, the first full year of the charter, the margin returns to the FY2025A level and the EBITDA margin recovers to 5.3%, so the -5.8pp move is a one-year transition, not a drift [S2][S16].

flags.message: a.gross_margin moves +5.4pp from FY2026E to FY2035E: source the change or hold it
flags.justification: FY2026E 14% is below the FY2025A 19.4% because H1 2026 actually ran at 4.9% gross margin (revenue USD17.69m against cost of revenue USD16.82m) and only H2 carries a full half of the BP charter [S9][S2]; FY2027E returns to the FY2025A 19.4%, the level management guided for 2026 ("di kisaran 20%") [S16]. The input is the margin at base input costs; the modelled gross-margin line is lower by the Brent bunker link (5% of COGS exposed, 30% passed through), which is why section 3 quotes the engine's gross-margin line and not the input [S0][S2].

flags.message: expected return -82%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The expected return is extreme because the equity has no cash value at the last actual margin and the target is carried almost entirely by the bull case. The drivers are sourced, not assumed: gross margin held at the FY2025A 19.4% (the level management guided to) [S0][S16], no funded vessel purchase because the only disclosed facility is a refinancing line [S16], a 9.0% cash cost of debt [S0], and a cost of capital of 9.9% WACC / 13.7% COE from the engine build [S0]. The reverse DCF answers the price: it requires FY2027E revenue growth of roughly 30% against our 12%, far above the company's own 18% target [S0][S16]. Bear and base both value the equity at zero and the bull at Rp61, so the probability weight on the bull is the whole judgement and is set out in section 5 [S0].

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_fcff': 0.6, 'ev_ebitda': 0.25, 'div_yield': 0.15}
flags.justification: Weights moved to a 100% DCF because neither earnings multiple is a usable anchor: LTM EBITDA is the FY2025A trough and H1 2026 has already made the year negative, so EV/EBITDA and P/E are computed on a denominator that no longer exists, and the own-history mean P/BV is inflated by the December 2025 price spike to Rp480 [S0][S6]. The adjusted_book method is not available on the corporate template, so the book cross-check is carried in the valuation section prose instead of as a weighted method, and the multiple diagnostics are reported without weight [S0].
